name: Wendy Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Wendy, and thanks for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Brookfield Community Farm, which is owned by a community land trust, so local people own the land together. About 300 households pay a yearly share and get a veg box every week, and alongside the vegetables we've got 30 beef cattle, a dozen sows and 400 laying hens on 60 hectares. I'm out at half six to feed the pigs and let the hens out, then I plan the day with my three staff and whatever volunteers turn up. Most mornings I've already asked my AI assistant to check the weather against the planting plan before I've finished my coffee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the Saturday pick-up, when the members come with their kids and I can say this is the field your carrots grew in. I love the puzzle of a good rotation, pigs clearing a field, then squash, then grain. What wears me down is the money. Membership dropped from 340 to 300 when food prices went up, and every household we lose is a bit of my staff's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because I use these tools every day and they're handy, not magic. I'd probably post that the real revolution in food is local, organic and owned by communities. At the trust board I'd say good, now let's get back to the membership numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my problem stays my problem. Brookfield lives on memberships, and people cut the veg box when money's tight. If we drop another 30 households, I'm cutting a staff member's hours or my own, and Sam and I still have a mortgage and two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the rotation plan, the newsletter and the seed order, because it saves me a good six hours a week. I'd use those hours to start paid school visits and weekend courses, charging per head for a day on pig keeping. And I'd join the regional network of community farms to share a marketing push for memberships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. A little restless, because I'd half hoped AI would help small farms more than it does in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said every lost household is a bit of your staff's wages. Who's most at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum, our youngest grower, he's 23 and on the shortest contract. He's brilliant with the pigs, and I'd fight hard for him. If it came to it, I'd cut my own hours before his, because I've got Sam's teacher's salary behind me and Callum's got nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the school visits look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Classes come out on a Tuesday, the kids collect eggs, meet the sows and dig potatoes they then take home. Schools pay per child, so twenty-five kids is a decent day for us. And some of those parents become members, which is the real point.

say: I'd say AI is **handy, not magic**, because I use it every day.
I'd post that the real food revolution is **local and community-owned**.
think: Brookfield lives on **memberships**, and they fall when money is tight.
Losing **30 more households** would mean cutting someone's hours, maybe mine.
do: Keep using **AI** for rotations, newsletters and seed orders.
Start **paid school visits** and weekend courses with the six hours saved.
Join the **regional community farm network** to push memberships together.
feel: **Fine**, but a little restless that AI doesn't help small farms more.
S0.quote: Brookfield lives on memberships, and people cut the veg box when money's tight.
fieldNote: Already an **everyday AI user**; for her the plateau is a disappointment, not a relief.
Money worry is **membership numbers**, which follow household budgets.
Would cut **her own hours** before her youngest grower's.
Leans on **Sam's teaching salary** as the household's backbone.

steps.text: Keep using AI for rotations, newsletters and seed orders
Start paid Tuesday school visits and weekend pig-keeping courses
Join the regional community farm network's membership drive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for small farms, if we're smart. AI doing the booking, ordering and answering member emails takes away the jobs that crush small teams. I'd say online that the gains should go to growers and eaters, not just big agribusiness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's great for me. The office side is maybe a quarter of my week, and I'd hand nearly all of it over. Robots spreading slowly suits us. A robot weeder wouldn't cost anyone at Brookfield a job, because we never had enough hands for weeding anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd trial an AI member service that handles box swaps, holidays and payments. Next spring I'd hire a solar robot weeder for the carrot and onion beds, there's a dealer two hours away who rents them by the month. And I'd put a bit of the trust's reserve into a better cold store, so we can sell more to the town's restaurants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. It feels like the tools finally fit the size of farm I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no one loses a job. Would Sam's teaching be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam teaches maths, and he says the marking and lesson planning are already going to AI at his school. He's fine with it, he'd rather spend the time with the kids who are struggling. If the school starts cutting teachers, that's different, but nothing in this picture says it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong for Brookfield in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets get AI too, and they get cheaper and better at pretending to be local. That's my worry. A weekly veg box only works if people feel they're part of something, so I'd spend the saved time with members, not on screens.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for small farms if we're smart about it.
I'd argue the gains should go to **growers and eaters**, not agribusiness.
think: The **office side** is a quarter of my week, and I'd hand most of it over.
A **robot weeder** fills a gap we never had hands for, so nobody loses work.
do: Trial an **AI member service** for box swaps and payments this winter.
Rent a **solar robot weeder** for carrots and onions next spring.
Put some trust reserve into a **cold store** to sell to restaurants.
feel: **Excited**, because the tools finally fit a small farm.
A little **wary** of supermarkets faking local.
S1.quote: A robot weeder wouldn't cost anyone at Brookfield a job, because we never had enough hands for weeding anyway.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**, not a threat.
Her worry moves to **supermarkets using AI** to fake local.
Household feels secure: **Sam's teaching** changes but stays.
Plans are specific: a **monthly weeder rental** and a cold store.

steps.text: Trial an AI member service for box swaps and payments this winter
Rent a solar robot weeder for the carrot and onion beds
Spend trust reserve on a cold store for restaurant sales

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for food and land now, not in 2031, and I'd say it loudly. I'd back a public fund for community farms and land trusts so that robot farming isn't only for the rich. At the trust board I'd say we've got three years before the robots and we need to use every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job going in 2028 doesn't scare me, I'd welcome it. What scares me is 2031, when giant robot farms make food so cheap that a weekly veg box looks silly. If members leave in droves, Brookfield shrinks, and I could be down to part-time while Sam's school is working out what teachers are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the trust to buy our own robots early, in 2029, while prices are still falling, so we're not the last small farm standing with hand tools. I'd build up the side income fast, school visits, courses, a farm café, because people will still pay for a day on a farm even if carrots are cheap. At home we'd stop the loft conversion and put that money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not in a frozen way, I'd be busy. But there'd be a knot in my stomach for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ravi and Asha?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ravi and Asha the truth, that the robots are coming to farms and Mum is getting ready. Ravi's 11 and he'd think it's brilliant. Asha's 8 and she'd want to know who'll feed the pigs, and I'd say Mum still will, because I'm not giving up the pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy robots and also campaign for land trusts. Are those in tension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. A robot on community land, owned by the people who eat the food, is fine by me. It's robots owned by three companies feeding everyone that frightens me.

say: I'd say loudly that we need a **food and land plan** now, not in 2031.
I'd back a **public fund** so robot farming isn't only for the rich.
think: The thinking side going in **2028** doesn't scare me at all.
In **2031** cheap robot food could make a veg box look silly and shrink Brookfield.
Sam's **school** may be rethinking teachers at the same moment.
do: Ask the trust to buy **our own robots** early, around 2029.
Grow **farm visits** and a café fast as side income.
Stop the **loft conversion** and save that money instead.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, with a knot in her stomach for three years.
S2.quote: A robot on community land, owned by the people who eat the food, is fine by me.
fieldNote: She welcomes thinking AI but fears **cheap robot food** wiping out the veg box.
Uses the **three-year gap** to buy robots and build visitor income.
Two-earner risk: both her farm and **Sam's school** face change.
Squares robots with progressive views through **community ownership**.

steps.text: Ask the land trust to buy its own robots around 2029
Open a farm café and expand school visits and courses
Shelve the loft conversion and save that money
Campaign for a public fund for community farms and land trusts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make community farms stronger, not weaker, if we plan. I'd say it at the regional network meeting and on the farm's newsletter. I'd say the land should stay with communities whatever machines are on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I had a proper runway. Thinking AI in 2031, robots in 2034, I'd be 51 and Asha would be 16. That's long enough to turn Brookfield into something people visit and learn at, not only buy from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd write a five-year plan with the board, using AI to model the numbers. I'd start a proper farm education programme with the county schools, paid by the school year. I'd take a course in robot maintenance, because if we buy robots in 2033, I want to fix them myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but focused. More like planning a hard harvest than bracing for a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your staff by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Callum running the education programme by then, because the kids love him. The other two growers would probably shift to robot care and the animals. I don't think we'd need fewer people, just different jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd carry on with the mortgage as normal, but put an extra bit into savings each month. Sam and I would talk about which of us has the safer job in 2034, and I honestly don't know the answer.

say: I'd say **five years** can make community farms stronger if we plan.
I'd say the **land should stay** with communities whatever machines are on it.
think: With robots in **2034** I'd be 51, with a proper runway to change.
Brookfield could become a place people **visit and learn**, not only buy from.
do: Write a **five-year plan** with the board, modelled with AI.
Start a paid **farm education programme** with county schools.
Take a **robot maintenance** course to fix our own machines.
feel: **Uneasy** but focused, like planning a hard harvest.
S3.quote: Sam and I would talk about which of us has the safer job in 2034, and I honestly don't know the answer.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **runway**, and she uses it immediately.
Pictures **different jobs, not fewer**, for her staff.
Admits real **household uncertainty** about which earner is safer.
Adaptive instinct: learn to **fix the robots** herself.

steps.text: Write a five-year plan with the trust board using AI models
Launch a paid farm education programme with county schools
Take a robot maintenance course before buying machines
Add a little extra to savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get this right, and I'd be cross if we didn't. I'd push the network to buy robots together around 2036. I'd say online that the future of food can be both high-tech and local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel quite good. I'd be 53 by 2039, the mortgage nearly paid, both kids done with school. I'd have a decade to make Brookfield the farm I'd want my kids to inherit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going much as now in the first year, using more AI as it improves. I'd put money aside in the trust's budget each year for robots, so in 2037 we can buy without a loan. And I'd keep growing the education side slowly, a few more schools a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you uneasy even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If big companies buy up the land around Brookfield for robot farms, land prices could jump. That would worry me. That's why I'd want the trust to buy the two fields next to us while it still can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the trust be able to afford them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, with a members' share offer, people buying a small piece of the farm. We did it once before for the barn. Ten years is enough to do it twice.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, and I'd be cross if we wasted it.
I'd post that food can be both **high-tech and local**.
think: By **2039** I'd be 53 with the mortgage nearly paid and kids through school.
A decade is time to make Brookfield a farm worth **inheriting**.
do: Keep going and use **more AI** as it improves.
Set aside **trust money** each year to buy robots without a loan in 2037.
Run a **members' share offer** to buy the two neighbouring fields.
S4.quote: If big companies buy up the land around Brookfield for robot farms, land prices could jump.
fieldNote: With a decade she is **calm and almost hopeful**.
Her one worry turns to **land prices** and outside buyers.
Plans to fund robots from **yearly savings**, not debt.
Thinks in terms of a farm her kids could **inherit**.

steps.text: Set aside trust money each year to buy robots in 2037
Run a members' share offer to buy the two neighbouring fields
Keep farming as now while using more AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because cheap robot food arrives in 2031 before community farms have had time to change. What would help is public money for land trusts and small farms to buy robots together, and schools paying properly for farm education. And honestly, protection for land, so it doesn't all end up with three companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what food is for. If robots make carrots nearly free, the reason to come to Brookfield isn't the carrot. People will still want to know where their food comes from and who grew it.

headlineQuote: If robots make carrots nearly free, the reason to come to Brookfield isn't the carrot.
portrait: **Wendy Patel**, 43, manages Brookfield, a **community-owned farm** feeding 300 households with veg boxes.
She uses **AI every day** and sees most change as a chance for small farms.
Her steady worry is **membership numbers**, which fall when household budgets tighten.
Fast AGI makes her anxious, because **cheap robot food** could empty the veg box list.
With more warning she plans **education, robots and land** under community ownership.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because cheap robot food arrives before community farms can change.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for land trusts to buy robots together.
Properly paid **farm education** and protection of land from big buyers.
